title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
titleZh: 美国 90% 的工作时间都花在了人工智能基准未涵盖的任务上
author: speckx
relevanceReason: 命中 4 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: The Benchmark MapEach tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks.All 22 job familiesclick a family to open itCoverage byCovered with at leastBenchmark IndexNo coverageAll 22 O*NET job families, with the share of their occupations covered by an AI benchmark.Job familyOccupations covered29 / 3633 / 4810 / 145 / 721 / 5121 / 5619 / 566 / 2213 / 4015 / 6012 / 899 / 621–12 of 22In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts, and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations.Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks. This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage billAdjusted probability of task coverageAnnualized occupation wage bill (log scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.Methodology in briefTo break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations.Example — 6 of the 22 tasks O*NET associates with Lawyers1Prepare, draft, and review legal documents, such as wills, deeds, patent applications, mortgages, leases, and contracts.2Advise clients concerning business transactions, claim liability, advisability of prosecuting or defending lawsuits, or legal rights and obligations.3Interpret laws, rulings and regulations for individuals and businesses.4Analyze the probable outcomes of cases, using knowledge of legal precedents.5Present evidence to defend clients or prosecute defendants in criminal or civil litigation.6Supervise legal assistants.To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:Public Availability. Included benchmarks have at least 25 publicly available tasks. We also include Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, where we have access to held-out benchmark prompts and are therefore able to map them to O*NET tasks.Agentic Tasks. Included benchmarks ask models to perform agentic tasks, rather than answering questions or advising the user on how to complete a task.Economic Realism. Benchmark tasks resemble tasks which humans (or agents) are frequently asked to do in real-world enterprises. Economically valuable tasks are prioritized over academically complex ones.Economic Diversity. We capped the number of included benchmarks per job family, in significant part to account for the massive overrepresentation of software engineering and research tasks in popular benchmarks.Balanced Difficulty. Benchmarks are not yet saturated by frontier models.Following work by Wang et al., we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al.’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab.LimitationsOur estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.Patterns in coverageThe benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al.), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation.But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts:Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage billAdjusted probability of task coverageAnnualized occupation wage bill (log scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important:Benchmark coverage by O*NET task importance within occupationsAdjusted probability of task coverageO*NET task importance (1–5 rating scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that, controlling for occupation, an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag and a given quintile O*NET importance score is covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Importance quintiles are calculated from O*NET importance scores. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and importance quintiles, with occupation fixed effects. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.The plots above suggest a reasonable allocation of the relatively limited resources devoted to high-quality, economically relevant benchmarks so far; it’s natural to prioritize making benchmarks which cover the most important and AI-exposed tasks in the occupations with the largest wage bills. But barring a significant increase in the number and diversity of such benchmarks, these patterns will result in significant blind spots in our view of economically valuable model capabilities.Can O*NET + benchmarks tell us how good AI is at your job?Measuring model capabilities by job occupation is essential – for enterprises deciding which models fit their needs, for policymakers forecasting the economic impact of AI, and for Americans thinking about their careers. Unfortunately, this is a hard problem to solve.We could just try averaging model performance on all benchmark prompts relevant to a given job. But as our Benchmark Map suggests, benchmarks cover some economic tasks much more intensively than others. A simple average would give too much weight to frequently benchmarked tasks.O*NET offers a way to potentially reduce this bias. If we average model performance on occupation-relevant benchmark prompts weighted by O*NET classification, so that each O*NET task is equally weighted in our occupation average, we get a step closer to a number that represents real economic performance.As a first step, we try this approach on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks for four occupations: investment banking, law, accounting, and software engineering. We compare O*NET-weighted scores to simple averages of model performance on tasks related to each occupation. The resulting weighted and unweighted scores are generally quite similar:APEX-1 + APEX-Agents · O*NET: Financial and Investment Analysts · 11 tasks · 176 promptsScore (%)Every prompt counts equallyEvery O*NET task counts equallyClaude Fable 5.1 Max69.8%68.5%Claude Opus 5.5 Max73.3%70.2%Claude Opus 5 Max65.5%63.0%GPT-6 Astra Max65.5%61.8%GPT-5.6 Sol Max66.8%65.6%Grok 4.7 xHigh58.1%58.7%Gemini 3.8 Flash High66.9%67.5%Kimi K3 Max59.4%59.9%DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Max56.5%58.4%For each occupation, we take all prompts across APEX benchmarks related to that occupation. Darker bars show a simple average of model scores on those prompts for each occupation. Then, we sort the prompts by O*NET task. For each O*NET task with at least 5 corresponding APEX prompts, we average model scores on those prompts to get a task-level score. Next, we average each task-level model score to get occupation-level scores which weight performance on each O*NET task equally. (If an O*NET task has fewer than 5 prompts, we drop it from the average). Lighter bars show these weighted scores for each occupation.In this case, at least, O*NET weighting changes very little. Model performance on APEX prompts is similar across the O*NET tasks included in the weighted scores above, which limits the value of reweighting. However, less than ⅓ of the O*NET tasks relevant to the 4 occupations above have enough APEX coverage to be included in our weighted scores. We are hopeful that applying O*NET weighting to a much larger set of benchmarks will result in high-quality occupation-specific model scores, and are working toward that goal.However, even if we incorporate tasks from dozens of benchmarks, several obstacles remain:01How do we navigate low statistical power?The sheer breadth of work done in the US economy means that for any O*NET occupation and task, we have relatively few benchmark items. This means that our estimates are inherently underpowered, and just one or two low-quality items can severely bias our scores.02How do we account for the varying difficulty and fidelity of tasks?Some benchmark items are highly saturated, whereas others are still unsolved. This is partly a function of time (as older benchmarks were designed for less performant models and simpler environments) and partly a function of quality (some benchmark items are simplistically graded, have minor mistakes, or can be reward hacked). We do not yet have an explicit way of weighting by quality.03Can evals that primarily measure AI automation generalize to augmentation?In the real world, AI models are still primarily used by humans, rather than automating entire job functions end-to-end. Therefore, measuring the real-world occupation capabilities of a model should ideally include measuring how much the model augments human productivity. We have completed some early work in this direction, but finding a methodology that scales remains elusive.04Can every O*NET occupation and task be measured with benchmarks?Knowledge-based work is well-suited to measurement through benchmarks because it is largely done on digital machines, like laptops and phones. Dingel and Neiman estimate that only 37% of US jobs could feasibly be done entirely from home, suggesting that ~63% of jobs involve some tasks with a physical-world component which would be hard to incorporate into current benchmarks. For now, this may not be a meaningful oversight – with the rapid development of robotics capabilities, we anticipate a significant need for physical task benchmarks.We are actively working on these problems; if you are too, please reach out!We are indebted to Wang et al. for the O*NET tagging methodology, and thank Nathan Lambert for feedback on a draft of this work.APEX NEWSLETTERThe latest on frontier AI performance, straight to your inbox.New benchmarks, leaderboard shifts, and research from the APEX team.

comments.author: b800h
comments.textRawHtml: Perhaps a version of the Doorman Fallacy, ie. replacing a doorman with an automatic door seems like an obvious win, but it turns out the doorman was performing a number of other vital functions (customer experience, for example) which weren't considered.
comments.textZhHtml: 也许是门卫谬误的一个版本，即。用自动门取代门卫似乎是一个明显的胜利，但事实证明门卫正在执行许多其他未被考虑的重要功能（例如客户体验）。

children.author: etempleton
children.textRawHtml:
This has been my argument for the past few weeks to explain why we aren’t seeing or feeling real world productivity gains as consumers despite many espousing the efficiency of AI they personally see with their own workflows. The hands on work is rarely the actual bottleneck.

My team can crank out high quality work in a few hours and AI could do the same medium to high quality work in a minute or two, but the review, feedback, and sign off takes days of back and forth. AI just slows this part of the process down because editing AI work is often a challenge because, no one is quite as familiar with how it was put together and sometimes it creates things that are not editable at all. And telling AI to make very specific changes is often a mixed bag at best.

Solo devs and small teams with minimal oversight can probably move a lot faster, but corporations are going to see minimal uplift except in areas where no one is looking.
children.textZhHtml:
这一直是我在过去几周的论点，以解释为什么我们作为消费者没有看到或感受到现实世界的生产力提高，尽管许多人拥护他们亲眼所见的人工智能在自己的工作流程中的效率。动手工作很少是真正的瓶颈。

我的团队可以在几个小时内完成高质量的工作，人工智能可以在一两分钟内完成相同的中等到高质量的工作，但审查、反馈和签署需要几天的时间来回。人工智能只是减慢了这部分过程，因为编辑人工智能工作通常是一项挑战，因为没有人非常熟悉它是如何组合在一起的，有时它会创建根本无法编辑的东西。告诉人工智能做出非常具体的改变往往是一个好坏参半的问题。

独立开发者和监督最少的小团队可能会移动得更快，但除了无人关注的领域之外，企业将看到最小的提升。

children.author: majormajor
children.textRawHtml:
Established successful companies operate in a world where action and change often introduce more immediate risk than staying still. In those companies AI doesn't necessarily offer a lot of "increased productivity" gains because writing the code isn't the bottleneck. But many of them will try to chase cost savings by laying people off or slowing hiring.

There's a couple types of companies where the reverse is true: young companies trying to grow, and dying ones that need a turnaround.

Out of those two, young companies are less likely to be set in their ways. So the first place you really see the result of development moving faster with AI is probably going to be in future months and years when suddenly-big companies start getting widely known with products and business strategies that wouldn't have made sense a decade ago because writing code to try different things to even get the ball rolling was a bottleneck, and you could only do things that wouldn't scale for so long.
children.textZhHtml:
对于成熟的成功公司来说，行动和变革往往比保持静止会带来更直接的风险。在这些公司中，人工智能不一定会带来很多“提高生产力”的收益，因为编写代码并不是瓶颈。但他们中的许多人会试图通过裁员或放慢招聘速度来节省成本。

有几种类型的公司情况恰恰相反：年轻的公司试图发展，而垂死的公司需要扭亏为盈。

在这两种公司中，年轻的公司不太可能按自己的方式行事。因此，你第一个真正看到 AI 带来的更快发展的结果可能是在未来的几个月和几年里，那时大公司突然开始以十年前没有意义的产品和业务策略而广为人知，因为编写代码来尝试不同的事情甚至让事情滚动是一个瓶颈，你只能做一些无法长期扩展的事情。

children.author: dingdongditchme
children.textRawHtml: Or the productivity gains, albeit substantial, are not as earth shattering as the llm providers would have you believe. As with any new technology adoption is a laggard. The internet "existed" in the late 80's, early 90's. Many companies are still reaping productivity gains from plugging into this first.
children.textZhHtml: 或者说，生产力的提高虽然很大，但并不像法学硕士提供商让您相信的那样是惊天动地的。与任何新技术一样，采用都是落后的。互联网“存在”于20世纪80年代末90年代初。许多公司仍然通过首先介入这一领域来获得生产力的提高。

children.author: lumost
children.textRawHtml:
I work in code generation, and often feel the fallacy of “because I can build something that looks 80% like your product in a day, you should pay me N millions.”

It's roughly the same pitch that the ruby on rails crowd had 15 years ago, and the no code crowd 5 years ago.

Very few companies need to rebuild their product every week, or actually care what tech stack it runs on. They are trying to build new things, or reduce how often those things break, or figuring out what if anything is worth building next.
children.textZhHtml:
我从事代码生成工作，经常感到这样的谬论：“因为我可以在一天内构建出与您的产品看起来 80% 相似的东西，您应该付给我 N 百万美元。”

这与 15 年前的 Ruby on Rails 人群和 5 年前的无代码人群的宣传大致相同。

很少有公司需要每周重建他们的产品，或者真正关心什么技术堆栈它继续运行。他们正在尝试构建新的事物，或者减少这些事物损坏的频率，或者弄清楚下一步是否值得构建什么。

children.author: thelastgallon
children.textRawHtml:
> Solo devs and small teams with minimal oversight can probably move a lot faster

Spot on!

Usually, most work in corps is slowed down by executive decisions. It takes 3 - 9 months to get a yes/no on something and for most things that are obvious that need to be done need to go up the chain of command. The decision takes forever, but when the decision is made, they want things to be done quickly, which creates unreasonable stress on the ICs.

The first step to see real productivity gains is for AI to eliminate the executive and middle-management layer, this starts a virtuous cycle, destroys both empire building and massively accelerates true productivity, not just meaningless metrics like LOC.
children.textZhHtml:
> 单独的开发人员和监督最少的小团队可能会进展得更快

完全正确！

通常，团队中的大多数工作都会因执行决策而减慢。需要 3 - 9 个月的时间才能对某件事做出是/否的决定，对于大多数明显需要完成的事情，都需要向上级指挥。决策需要很长时间，但当决策做出后，他们希望事情能够快速完成，这对 IC 造成了不合理的压力。

看到真正生产力提升的第一步是人工智能消除执行层和中层管理层，这会启动一个良性循环，破坏帝国建设并大幅加速真正的生产力，而不仅仅是像 LOC 这样毫无意义的指标。

children.author: somenameforme
children.textRawHtml:
Speaking realistically, you're going in the wrong direction here. The most likely scenario in the short run is that management will seek to replace labor with automated systems supported by a skeleton crew to aid in implementation and execution level tasks that can't (or shouldn't) be handled by the LLM alone, like deployment.

So the first signs of productivity gains will be shrinking head count, but it's going go from the bottom up, as usual.
children.textZhHtml:
说实话，你在这里走错了方向。短期内最有可能的情况是，管理层将寻求用由骨干人员支持的自动化系统取代劳动力，以帮助实施和执行级别的任务，这些任务不能（或不应该）由法学硕士单独处理，例如部署。

因此，生产力提高的第一个迹象将是减少员工人数，但它会像往常一样从下到上进行。

children.author: abustamam
children.textRawHtml:
I considered it an absolute win when I submitted an LLM assisted PR that removed 30k LOC :)

> most work in corps is slowed down by executive decisions

I work in a startup and I find it to be the opposite. Management wants us to go really fast and engineering is like "well wait we should slow down because just because LLMs can write a bunch of code doesn't mean it can build a maintainable app"

That said, I know that our small engineering team can't build an entire business by ourselves. So some management is required. But as you said, getting stuff done quickly is stressful. And with LLMs we're expected to get a LOT of stuff done very quickly. Some colleagues have decided to go on quiet strike by submitting AI slop and citing "no time to review" to prove a point. I don't fault them, but I also know that me and someone else will have to clean up their messes at some point.
children.textZhHtml:
当我提交了一份 LLM 辅助 PR 并删除了 30k LOC 时，我认为这是绝对的胜利:)

> 团队中的大多数工作都因执行决策而减慢

我在一家初创公司工作，我发现情况恰恰相反。管理层希望我们走得非常快，而工程就像“好吧，我们应该放慢速度，因为法学硕士可以编写一堆代码并不意味着它可以构建一个可维护的应用程序”

也就是说，我知道我们的小型工程团队无法独自构建整个业务。所以需要一些管理。但正如你所说，快速完成工作会带来压力。通过法学硕士，我们预计能够很快完成很多工作。一些同事决定以“没有时间审查”为由，通过提交人工智能废液来证明这一点，从而进行安静的罢工。我不会责怪他们，但我也知道我和其他人在某个时候必须清理他们的烂摊子。

children.textZhHtml:
人工智能。首席执行官们。现在。
您使用的是什么型号？我发现 Claude Sonnet 非常有能力生成正确的查询。另外，您是否使用语义层 [1]，因为如果没有它，模型可能无法理解您的模式。如果您私信这些设置得到了错误的答案，我会感到非常惊讶。我从未见过 Sonnet 4.6+ 产生错误的查询。

2）当时和现在受雇担任门卫的人口比例是多少？

3）当时和现在有多少人口受益于门卫？

这与 15 年前的 Ruby on Rails 人群和 5 年前的无代码人群的宣传大致相同。

很少有公司需要每周重建他们的产品，或者真正关心什么技术堆栈它继续运行。他们正在尝试构建新的事物，或者减少这些事物损坏的频率，或者弄清楚下一步是否值得构建什么。

按照这些公司的结构方式，我们看到他们解雇了从事实际工作的人员，而没有人想惹恼高管。我的公司大约有 60 个 EVP 头衔，依次为高级副总裁、副总裁、高级总监和董事。 几乎所有副总裁及以上级别的人都可能消失，我们的生活会更轻松。它造成了大量的政治活动和帝国建设，阻碍了公司和个人，然后交付代码和产品的个人成为效率指标的目标，高层没有任何变化。

我不知道它如何可持续，但我不认为人工智能首席执行官会出现，直到一家新公司使用该模型从底层取得成功。

I have no idea how it’s sustainable but I dont see AI CEOs coming until a new company becomes successful from the bottom using that model.

children.author: leftouterjoins
children.textRawHtml:
This is my experience. As a data engineer with years in my current role I can get AI to write good SQL that correctly answers questions or defines metrics. At worst it may take a few back and forths to really nail it.

However, if a PM tries it they will more often than not get a wrong answer because they do not know what to look for or how to ask the right questions.

Prompts still matter a lot especially when you are working in an established enterprise.
children.textZhHtml:
这是我的经验。作为一名在当前职位上工作多年的数据工程师，我可以让 AI 编写出良好的 SQL 来正确回答问题或定义指标。在最坏的情况下，可能需要反复几次才能真正解决问题。

但是，如果产品经理尝试这样做，他们往往会得到错误的答案，因为他们不知道要寻找什么或如何提出正确的问题。

提示仍然很重要，尤其是当您在成熟的企业中工作时。

children.author: weinzierl
children.textRawHtml:
I know the Doorman Fallacy is an established concept, but where did it really ever apply? The automatic door has won despite, devastatingly so (and no your fancy upper east side building doesn't count and neither does the Regency or the Hilton).

The doorman was called a doorman because its essential task was the door. Everything else was additional and replaceable or unnecessary in the first place.

Same with AI. Once it has replaced the main task, the rest will adapt around it.
children.textZhHtml:
我知道门卫谬误是一个既定的概念，但它真正适用于哪里？尽管如此，自动门还是取得了毁灭性的胜利（不，你那精美的上东区建筑不算在内，摄政酒店或希尔顿酒店也不算在内）。

门卫被称为门卫，因为它的基本任务是门。首先，其他一切都是额外的、可替换的或不必要的。

人工智能也是如此。一旦它取代了主要任务，其余的就会围绕它进行调整。

children.author: CodeyWhizzBang
children.textRawHtml:
When you say the automatic door "has won" do you mean it's won by rendering doormen obsolete? Because if so, that seems very untrue. According to Vanity Fair and NPR there are over 25,000 doormen working in New York City. 1930 there were an estimated few thousand. So since the invention of the automatic door, the number of doormen has skyrocketed.

Maybe, you'd say there are more automatic doors than doormen. I'm confident that is true, but those automatic doors haven't supplanted doormen; they're automatic doors where there would have been manual doors before.

So everything hasn't adapted around automatic doors. We've just got a lot more automatic doors now. And a lot more doormen.
children.textZhHtml:
当您说自动门“获胜”时，您的意思是通过淘汰门卫而赢得胜利吗？因为如果是这样，那就显得非常不真实了。据 Vanity Fair 和 NPR 报道，纽约市有超过 25,000 名门卫。 1930 年估计有几千人。所以自从自动门发明以来，门卫的数量猛增。

也许，你会说自动门比门卫还多。我相信这是真的，但那些自动门并没有取代门卫；它们是自动门，以前有手动门。

所以一切都还没有适应自动门。我们现在有了更多的自动门。还有更多的门卫。

3) What proportion of the population benefited from doormen then and now?
